discussion_comments.comment_body: We receive a steady stream of ~~beg bounties~~reports to PSRT about private keys being present in bugs.python.org, etc. A compromised private key would likely invite even more attention, can we obfuscate this in a way that prevents that from happening?

yeah I was thinking the same thing based on past reports.  also, distrusted_keycert.pem looks like a premade cert signed with the distrusted private key... rather than checking that hazmat-ish thing into our tree, could the test wanting that just generate one at runtime when an `openssl` command is available (too slow? we can tag it as `@support.requires_resource('cpu')` ).

I like that the filenames clearly have distrusted_ in their name.  I wish things scanning for private key strings would grow up and learn to not report things like this but they tend to be a trivial grep.

It's two ECC genkey operations and one ECC signing operation. That is incredible fast, maybe 10ms in total on a recent computer.

Is this really worth the trouble and extra complications? "Security scanners" are already complaining about the private RSA keys. And they will start to complain about the eMudhra CA certs, too. I could obfuscate the files with ROT13 or put them in a password-protected zip file (`Brave Sir Robin`?).

The problem is really the dumb scanners that do stuff like blocking git push - I have to jump through all sorts of hoops to admin-override checks just to maintain a mirror at work, and then I also have to go and add comments to all these files to satisfy _another_ scanner that this isn't a real secret (or else they're going to _contact my manager_ 😟 ).

But yeah, even something that separates the header from the base 64 and writes the key file out just for the test would be a huge pain relieved from my perspective. Even renaming to `.txt` may well work, though I haven't tried that. I assume others face similar issues.
Looks like the PR now uses an encrypted zip to store the certs, does that address the concerns?
Oh, I forgot to submit my comment.... sry. I addressed the concerns in the morning by moving the certs and private key to an encrypted ZIP file. Brave Sir Robin to the rescue!
